basePrompt: Use case: infographic-diagram. Asset type: one educational illustration inside a Rust example guide. Make a polished LANDSCAPE infographic with a dark navy backdrop, mint and coral accents, cream readable typography, restrained flat editorial illustration and precise diagrams. Title is the example title given below. Use generously spaced panels, large labels, thin arrows showing true data flow. Readable on a phone, no watermark, no clutter, no invented results. All numeric values and text specified below are exact.

examples.diagram: Show program data fuel 82%, signal 67%, oxygen 94% leading to ui::bar(value) and then formatted stdout. Use ONE ten-cell bar per value, only in the middle panel: 8 filled and 2 empty for fuel, 6 filled and 4 empty for signal, 9 filled and 1 empty for oxygen. Output panel shows only three labels and their exact percentages, NO repeated bars.
examples.caption: Ten-cell bars truncate to whole cells; the original percentages remain unchanged.
examples.alt: Ten-cell bars truncate to whole cells; the original percentages remain unchanged.

examples.diagram: 32-bit seed 0xC0FFEE -> wrapping multiply 1_664_525 and add 1_013_904_223 -> separate terminal 38x12 and canvas64x40 sequences. Terminal remainder29 chooses bright/dim/space. Canvas upper16bits selects coordinates and dither. Effects: faint haze, two-cell halos, one static meteor trail. No animation loop.
examples.caption: A 32-bit seed drives two repeatable views: a 38 by 12 terminal grid and a 64 by 40 pixel canvas with faint haze, star halos, and a static meteor trail.
examples.alt: Seeded 32-bit sequence branches into a text star field and a color canvas. The canvas layers diagonal haze, separated stars, small halos and one meteor trail.

examples.diagram: Show phrase 'rust makes systems fearless rust makes ideas real' -> split_whitespace -> BTreeMap. Final alphabetical frequency table exactly: fearless 1, ideas 1, makes 2, real 1, rust 2, systems 1. Use six labeled proportional bars. Footer: Exact spelling is the key.
examples.caption: Whitespace-separated words are counted by exact spelling and emitted in sorted BTreeMap key order.
examples.alt: Whitespace-separated words are counted by exact spelling and emitted in sorted BTreeMap key order.

examples.diagram: Four clean rows demonstrating classify(value) via pair (value % 3, value % 5): 15 -> (0,0) -> FizzBuzz; 9 -> (0,4) -> Fizz; 10 -> (1,0) -> Buzz; 7 -> (1,2) -> 7. First joint-zero case highlighted. Footer: Every match arm has a result.
examples.caption: Matching two remainders makes the combined, individual, and ordinary-number cases explicit.
examples.alt: Matching two remainders makes the combined, individual, and ordinary-number cases explicit.

examples.diagram: Two formula cards 'F = C * 9 / 5 + 32' and 'K = C + 273.15' leading into a neat three-column table C | F | K. Rows exactly -20.0 | -4.0 | 253.15; 0.0 | 32.0 | 273.15; 30.0 | 86.0 | 303.15. Show formatting-width guides. Footer: Compute first, format second.
examples.caption: Celsius values feed the Fahrenheit and Kelvin formulas; width and precision create an aligned report.
examples.alt: Celsius values feed the Fahrenheit and Kelvin formulas; width and precision create an aligned report.

examples.diagram: Illustrate sieve limited to 20 for clarity, not the full 200 runtime example. Ordered stages: candidates 2..20; mark multiples of 2 starting at 4; mark multiples of 3 starting at 9; survivors. Final survivor list exactly '2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19'. Clearly exclude 0 and 1. Footer: Start marking at p * p. Avoid an incorrectly colored giant grid; show lists and arrows.
examples.caption: A small limit of 20 shows how marking multiples from each prime's square leaves the prime candidates.
examples.alt: A small limit of 20 shows how marking multiples from each prime's square leaves the prime candidates.

examples.diagram: A reversible number-conversion diagram for 14. Forward: 14 -> 10 + 4 -> X + IV -> XIV. Reverse: XIV -> 10 - 1 + 5 -> 14. Footnote: Decoder does not validate canonical spelling. Keep arrows directionally accurate.
examples.caption: A descending value table encodes 14 as XIV; subtractive decoding returns 10 minus 1 plus 5.
examples.alt: A descending value table encodes 14 as XIV; subtractive decoding returns 10 minus 1 plus 5.

examples.diagram: Two matrices A = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]] and B = [[7,8],[9,10],[11,12]], leading to C = [[58,64],[139,154]]. Highlight A's first row and B's first column. One formula 'C[0][0] = 1*7 + 2*9 + 3*11 = 58'. Dimension labels 2x3 times 3x2 gives 2x2. No other calculations.
examples.caption: Each output cell is a row-column dot product; the illustrated first cell is 58.
examples.alt: Each output cell is a row-column dot product; the illustrated first cell is 58.

examples.diagram: Flow: terminal cell -> complex coordinate c -> repeated z = z*z + c, starting z = 0 -> escape count -> character shade -> ASCII fractal. Label 'escape when |z|^2 > 4' and 'limit 60'. Render the fractal as symbolic ASCII texture, not a mathematically exact plot. Footer: 64 columns x 24 rows.
examples.caption: Each terminal cell samples a complex coordinate and maps its escape count to one of eight characters.
examples.alt: Each terminal cell samples a complex coordinate and maps its escape count to one of eight characters.

examples.diagram: Use a 3-stage cellular automaton explanation with a 3x3 neighbor stencil highlighting eight neighbors around a center. Rule cards exactly: Alive + 2 or 3 neighbors -> Alive; Dead + 3 neighbors -> Alive; Other cases -> Dead. Show current grid -> separate next grid. Footer: 32 x 16 grid; edges wrap. Do not create an inaccurate glider evolution sequence.
examples.caption: Eight neighbors determine birth and survival; a separate output grid keeps each generation consistent.
examples.alt: Eight neighbors determine birth and survival; a separate output grid keeps each generation consistent.

examples.caption: Owned optional children form a recursive tree whose in-order traversal returns sorted values.
examples.alt: Owned optional children form a recursive tree whose in-order traversal returns sorted values.

examples.alt: The three enum states cycle deterministically; their durations place the next red state at 60 seconds.

examples.diagram: Flow: CSV rows -> parse -> Option<Sale> -> filter_map -> regional totals. Show example row 'north, keyboard, 12, 49.99', calculation '12 * 49.99 = 599.88'. Separate warning 'Invalid rows are skipped; quoted commas are unsupported'. Do not invent a complete CSV parser.

examples.alt: Each accepted row becomes a Sale; per-row totals are summed by region while malformed rows are skipped.

examples.diagram: Input '10 / 2.5' -> peekable character scan -> three distinct tokens 'Number(10.0)', 'Slash', 'Number(2.5)'. Separate error example '1 + $' -> 'unexpected character: $'. Footer: Tokens only; no evaluation. Use no computed answer4.

examples.diagram: Show Stack<&str> with bottom rust, middle is, top explicit. push arrow points into top, pop arrow out of top. Pop sequence explicit -> is -> rust -> None. A peek call points at top without removal. Footer: Vec<T> provides reusable storage.

examples.diagram: Flow of six log rows -> filter_map -> parsed tuples -> report. Four metrics exactly 'requests 6', 'succeeded 4', 'total time 149 ms', 'slowest /login 51 ms'. Explain status200 successes only; all parsed durations count in total. No ranked-all-requests chart.

examples.alt: Mapping three expense records to their amounts and summing them produces the formatted total 1018.90.

examples.alt: A fixed task array uses three enum statuses; filtering Done counts one completed task out of three.
